897.title: Whitefield in the fields
897.hook: a cross-eyed actor-preacher heard by crowds in the open air
897.howItsDone: Open-air preaching is still part of some evangelical and Methodist life, from street corners to summer camp meetings, and Whitefield is remembered by Anglicans, Methodists and evangelicals as a leading open-air preacher of the revival.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles Wesley's hymns, among them Love divine, and your line: o for a thousand tongues.

A printer in Philadelphia is walking backward down a crowded street. Not for fun. He's measuring. Up the street, a young preacher stands on the courthouse steps, talking to a crowd packed into the open air, and the printer wants to know how far one voice can carry before the noise of the city swallows it. No roof, no pews, no organ. Just weather, and a voice. The printer is Benjamin Franklin. The preacher is an Anglican clergyman with a squint in one eye and, as a boy, a love of the stage.

George Whitefield belonged to the same circle at Oxford as John and Charles Wesley, the group their classmates mocked as the Methodists. When pulpits in England stopped inviting him, he walked out to a hillside where coal miners came up from the pits, and preached to whoever was standing there. Tradition says tears ran pale lines down the coal dust on their faces. A respectable clergyman didn't preach outside. Whitefield did it anyway, then talked John Wesley into trying it too. He crossed the ocean again and again, preaching through the American colonies in fields, town squares and market streets. What did he say? One line he came back to was Jesus's word in the Gospel of John: "Ye must be born again." Not a new church, not a new rule, but a new heart. People said he could make a crowd weep by the way he spoke a single word. Then there's Franklin, no revivalist himself. In his autobiography, he tells how he went to hear Whitefield having decided not to give a penny to the collection. As the sermon went on he softened, first to copper coins, then to silver, and in the end, he writes, he emptied his pocket into the dish. The walk backward comes from the same book. The field preaching raised hard questions too. Some ministers said he stirred up feelings and left the churches to clean up after him. And later in life he owned enslaved people on a Georgia estate; that belongs in his story too. The open air took the sermon out of the building, to the pit head, the courthouse steps and the market.

Sit up, let your shoulders drop, and breathe low into your belly. On one out-breath, say a single sentence out loud at full voice, as if to someone across a field: your name, a line you love, or, if you pray, a line from a psalm you know. Then sit in the quiet after it, and listen to how far the silence goes.
Born again. Whitefield's central message to every crowd: not a new church or rule, but a new heart, as Jesus told Nicodemus.
Your line: in the open air. No roof needed, just weather and a voice. Day eight hundred ninety-seven, done.

898.title: Jonathan Edwards
898.hook: the Great Awakening in New England, and Edwards writing on religious affections
898.howItsDone: Edwards is read in Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist and evangelical churches and seminaries, and his Religious Affections is still used by pastors trying to tell real spiritual awakening from passing excitement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, born again: Whitefield preaching a new heart in the fields. Your line was in the open air.

Honey on the tongue. You can read that honey is sweet, repeat it, pass a test on it. Or you can taste it. Same fact, two different kinds of knowing. A pastor in a small New England town used that picture, the taste of honey, to describe faith. Then his own church was stirred up: people weeping, staying up late to pray, crowding his study with questions. Some neighbors called it a work of God. Others called it hysteria. He decided the honest thing was to sit down and think it through.

Jonathan Edwards was a Congregationalist minister in Northampton, Massachusetts, during the season of revival people later called the Great Awakening, the same stirring Whitefield preached into. He's often remembered for one frightening sermon about sinners in the hands of an angry God. But much of his life went into a harder question: when a revival sweeps through a town, how do you tell what is real? He answered in a long book, A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections. Its claim is short: "True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections." By affections he didn't mean passing moods. He meant the deep leanings of the heart: what a person loves, hates, hopes for and delights in. In a sermon on a divine and supernatural light, he drew the difference that gives us our line. There's believing, as a matter of opinion, that God is holy and gracious, and there's having a sense of the heart, tasting it, the way someone who has eaten honey knows its sweetness as a reader never will. Then the careful part. Edwards warned that strong feelings prove nothing on their own. Tears, shaking, loud joy: none of them, he argued, settle whether something is from God. The chief sign, he wrote, is a changed life, the fruit of the heart showing up in ordinary practice, day after day. So he defended the feelings against the scoffers, and tested them against the enthusiasts. A sense of the heart, yes. Then watch what it does on Monday.
screen: `HOW DO YOU TELL WHAT IS REAL?`

segments.voice: Sit, breathe slowly, and ask quietly: what am I leaning toward right now, and what am I leaning away from? Don't fix anything; just name it the way you'd name a taste: wanting, dreading, delighting, longing. If you pray, hold what you find before God without dressing it up; if you don't, simply notice the leaning.
Jonathan Edwards. A New England pastor in the Great Awakening who wrote that true religion lives in holy affections, and that a changed life is the best test of them.
Your line: a sense of the heart. Tasted, not just read about. See you tomorrow.

899.title: Joy to the world
899.hook: Isaac Watts wrote it as a psalm (Psalm 98), not originally for Christmas
899.howItsDone: Joy to the World is sung in Protestant and Catholic churches, usually at Christmas, though some churches also sing it in Advent or at other seasons as a hymn of Christ's rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonathan Edwards and his test for revival: a changed life. Your line was a sense of the heart.

A carol plays in a grocery store in December, between the canned cranberries and the wrapping paper. Joy to the world, the Lord is come. It gets filed under Christmas. Now listen to the words. No manger, no shepherds, no star, no wise men, no baby at all. There's earth, heaven, fields and floods, rocks, hills and plains, and a king who rules the world. It reads less like a nativity scene than a coronation. That's because it began as something else.

Isaac Watts was an English minister among the Dissenters, the Protestants outside the Church of England. In his day, some of those churches sang only the Psalms, in versions kept close to the Bible's wording. Watts thought Christians should sing the Psalms the way a Christian would pray them, with Jesus in view. So he rewrote the Psalms in his own verse, and Joy to the world is his version of Psalm 98. Open the King James Bible to that psalm and you can hear the bones of the hymn: "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all the earth: make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise." A little further, the sea roars, the floods clap their hands, the hills are joyful together. Why? Because the Lord comes to judge the earth: "with righteousness shall he judge the world, and the people with equity." Watts opened his hymn: "Joy to the world! the Lord is come; Let earth receive her King." For Watts the coming king is Jesus, and the hymn looks toward his rule over all the earth. Christians read that coming more than one way. Some hear the first coming, the birth, which is why it found a home at Christmas. Others hear the coming at the end of the age, when the world is set right. Watts didn't write it for any one season. And look at the line that becomes ours. Let earth receive her king. Not the church, not the good people. The earth: fields and floods, rocks and hills. The whole created world is invited to make room.
screen: `THE PSALMS, SUNG WITH JESUS IN VIEW.`

segments.voice: Out of season is the point: say to yourself what today actually is, an ordinary day with no tinsel, and sing the first line into it, quietly or out loud. Then let the psalm's list go by in your mind, one at a time: the sea, the floods, the hills. If you pray, make the last line yours, let earth receive her king; if you don't, notice the earth under you, holding you up.
Isaac Watts. The English minister who rewrote the Psalms with Jesus in view, turning Psalm 98 into the hymn Joy to the world.
Your line: let earth receive her king. Any day of the year. That's day eight hundred ninety-nine.

900.title: Amazing grace
900.hook: John Newton, a slave-ship captain, later becomes a pastor and joins the abolitionists
900.howItsDone: Amazing Grace is sung across Protestant, Catholic and other churches, at Sunday services, funerals and public gatherings, and Newton is remembered in the Church of England's story of the campaign against the slave trade.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaac Watts, whose Joy to the world was a psalm before it was a carol. Your line was let earth receive her king.

Wretch is a strange word to find in a song people sing at funerals and at weddings. That saved a wretch like me. The man who wrote it didn't mean it as a figure of speech. He had been a sailor, a slave trader, and the captain of ships that carried captured Africans across the Atlantic in chains. Later he became a pastor in a small English village. Later still, he stood up in public, said the trade he had worked in was wicked, and wanted it ended.

John Newton's story is often told as a sudden turn: a storm at sea, a terrified prayer, a changed man. That storm did matter to him. But the honest version is slower and harder. After it, Newton kept working in the slave trade, and even captained slave ships, while reading his Bible and keeping a prayer journal. Faith came first. Seeing what he had done came much later. In time he left the sea, was ordained in the Church of England, and served as curate in the village of Olney, where he and the poet William Cowper wrote hymns for their congregation. That's where Amazing grace comes from: "Amazing grace! (how sweet the sound) That sav'd a wretch like me! I once was lost, but now am found, Was blind, but now I see." Listen for the Gospels in it. Lost and found is the father's cry over the prodigal son in Luke: "he was lost, and is found." Blind but now I see is the man Jesus healed in John, answering his questioners: "whereas I was blind, now I see." Then Newton did something harder than writing a hymn. Years after leaving the trade, he published a pamphlet describing what he had seen on the ships, confessing he had taken part, and condemning the trade. He supported William Wilberforce and the campaign to end it. Grace, in Christian teaching, is God's love freely given, never earned. In Newton's life it didn't erase the past. It made him able, finally, to look at it.

Think of a wrong you once defended: something you argued for, excused or laughed along with, that you see differently now. Name it plainly to yourself, without excuse and without beating yourself up. If you pray, bring it to God in your own words, or with Newton's line, I once was lost.
Amazing grace. John Newton's hymn, written by a former slave-ship captain turned pastor: I once was lost, but now am found, was blind, but now I see.
Your line: I once was lost. But now am found. Nine hundred days, and counting.

901.title: The Philokalia (1782)
901.hook: two Greek monks gather the Orthodox writings on inner prayer into one collection
901.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians may pray the Jesus Prayer with a prayer rope, a cord of knots, saying the prayer once on each knot, ideally under the guidance of a priest or spiritual father or mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amazing grace: a slave-ship captain who finally looked at his past. Your line was I once was lost.

Advice from desert hermits. Notes from abbots on watching your thoughts. Short teachings on how to keep praying while you work, walk and eat. For generations, monks copied these out by hand, and they sat scattered across monastery libraries, in manuscripts few people could ever see. Then two monks decide it should all be in one place, printed, where anyone who wanted it could find it. They give their anthology a name that sounds less like a manual than a love letter.

The two monks were Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain, from Mount Athos, and Makarios of Corinth, a bishop. Their book gathers writings by Orthodox teachers across the centuries on what the Orthodox call watchfulness: guarding the heart, noticing thoughts as they arrive, and praying inwardly. The title is Greek, and it carries our line: Philokalia, love of the beautiful, or love of the good. The beautiful here isn't a painting. It's God, and a heart made quiet enough to love God. At the center of much of the book is a very short prayer, the Jesus Prayer. Orthodox Christians pray it in words like these: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. It grows out of the Gospels. In Luke, a blind man by the road near Jericho calls out, "Jesus, thou Son of David, have mercy on me." And in Jesus's parable the tax collector stands far off in the temple and prays only, "God be merciful to me a sinner." Paul tells the Thessalonians: "Pray without ceasing." How do you do that? You give the mind one short prayer, said slowly, often with the breath, until it's less something you say and more something the heart keeps saying. The writers are honest that this isn't a technique for calm. They warn against chasing experiences, and they say a beginner needs a guide. Catholics have their own long tradition of contemplative prayer, and some Protestants pray short breath prayers too. But this collection comes from the Orthodox, and the way of prayer it teaches is theirs.

Sit still and let your breathing slow. If you pray, say the Jesus Prayer silently, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, on the in-breath, have mercy on me, on the out-breath, and when your mind wanders, come back without fuss. If you don't pray, simply breathe, and on each out-breath let the word mercy pass through.
Philokalia. A Greek word meaning love of the beautiful, and the name of an Orthodox anthology on inner prayer and watchfulness of the heart.
Your line: love of the beautiful. One short prayer, said slowly. Day nine hundred one, done.

902.title: Paisius Velichkovsky
902.hook: a Ukrainian monk translates the Philokalia into Slavonic and renews Russian monasteries
902.howItsDone: In Orthodox Christianity, people may have a spiritual father or mother, often a priest or monastic, to whom they bring their thoughts and confession, and some travel to monasteries to ask an elder for guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Philokalia, the Orthodox anthology on inner prayer. Your line was love of the beautiful.

On Mount Athos, the Holy Mountain in Greece, a monk from Ukraine sits with two texts side by side. One is an old Slavonic translation of a Greek writer on prayer. The other is the Greek itself. They don't match. Copyists have muddled the Slavonic until some sentences barely make sense. He had walked out of a theological academy in Kyiv without finishing, not failing, just restless: the lectures were full of argument, and he wanted to learn how to pray. Now the books his own people pray from turn out to be blurred. So he sets out to learn Greek properly and fix them.

Paisius had looked for a living teacher of prayer and, by his own account, mostly failed to find one. So he learned Greek well enough to read the old writers on prayer for himself. Other monks began gathering around him, first on Athos and later in monasteries in Moldavia, in what is now Romania. He ran those communities in two languages, so Slavic and Romanian monks could both follow the services and readings. And he gave his life to translation. Working from Greek manuscripts, he rendered the teachings of the Philokalia into Church Slavonic, the language of worship in the Russian and other Slavic churches. Now a Russian monk who had never seen Athos could read the desert fathers on watchfulness and the Jesus Prayer. Paisius never went to Russia to lead it himself. His disciples carried his books and his way of life north, and with them came our line: the startsy. A starets, in Russian, is an elder, a monk whose long practice of prayer lets him guide others. You go to him, open your heart, tell him your thoughts, and he gives a word for you. It isn't a lecture. It's a relationship, closer to a doctor and a patient, or a parent and a child. Paisius taught that obedience to a wise guide protects a beginner on the road into inner prayer, because a beginner left alone easily fools himself. Through his disciples, elders became a living presence in Russian monasteries, and ordinary people, peasants and nobles, began making journeys to ask them for a word. The restless student who couldn't find a teacher helped form the teachers who followed.

Bring to mind someone older or wiser who has helped you: a grandparent, a teacher, a pastor, a friend who's been through things. Hear their voice, and remember one thing they said that stayed. If you pray, give thanks for them or pray for them by name; if you don't, just hold them with gratitude.
Paisius Velichkovsky. A Ukrainian monk who translated the Philokalia into Church Slavonic and whose disciples carried the tradition of elders into Russian monasteries.

903.title: Tikhon of Zadonsk
903.hook: a bishop who gave away his bishop's comforts to live simply among the poor
903.howItsDone: The Orthodox Church remembers Tikhon of Zadonsk as a saint with feast days in its calendar, and his writings on prayer and on seeing God in ordinary things are still read in Orthodox homes and monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paisius Velichkovsky and the elders his disciples carried to Russia. Your line was the startsy.

There's a story told about a Russian bishop and a quarrel. A proud nobleman, losing an argument with him, struck him across the face. The bishop didn't strike back, and didn't storm out. Tradition says he bowed down to the floor in front of the man and asked his forgiveness for having provoked him. The nobleman, shaken, ended up on his knees too. This bishop had already stepped away from what a bishop gets: the palace, the standing, the comforts.
screen: `A BISHOP WHO GAVE IT ALL UP.`

segments.voice: Tikhon was a Russian Orthodox bishop who served the diocese of Voronezh. He worked hard at it, opening schools and teaching his clergy, until his health broke down. Then he asked to step aside, and went to live in a monastery at Zadonsk, near the river Don. There he lived very simply, in a plain cell, and gave away what came to him, food, clothes, money, to the poor who lined up at his door. He visited prisoners. He sat with peasants. People came to him for counsel, as they would to one of the elders we met yesterday. His writings return again and again to one habit of mind: everything around you can point to God, even the plainest things you pass every day. He wrote a book on just that, gathering spiritual lessons from ordinary things. It leads to our line: all is from God. Tikhon didn't mean that every cruelty is God's wish. He meant that nothing, not even trouble, falls outside God's care, so a person can receive good days and bad ones with trust. It echoes Paul's letter to the Romans: "all things work together for good to them that love God." It also sheds light on the bow after the slap. If even an insult can be received from God's hand, then, as Tikhon saw it, there was no need to defend his dignity with his fists. The Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky admired him, and some readers see Tikhon behind the gentle elder Zosima in The Brothers Karamazov. The Orthodox Church honors him as a saint.

Let go of one small comfort you'd normally reach for right now, the cushion, the snack, the extra blanket, and sit without it, noticing what you feel. If you pray, offer the small lack to God, or think of someone who goes without every day; if you don't, notice the gap, and think of who might use what you didn't.
Tikhon. The Russian bishop who stepped aside from a grand life, lived simply at Zadonsk, and taught that everything can point to God.

Your line: all is from God. That ends a week of preachers, poets and monks: Whitefield's born again, Edwards and the heart, Isaac Watts's hymn, Amazing grace, the Philokalia, Paisius, and Tikhon. A week, done.
